around.summary: A boy was attacked and stabbed by two men on a scooter while heading to tuition in Bengaluru; the attackers fled the scene. If you supervise children on this route, consider group travel or an adult escort until police establish more details.

around.headline: Software professional arrested for secretly filming his landlady
around.summary: A tenant was arrested after allegedly installing a hidden camera and filming his landlady in the bathroom of the house he rented a room in. It's a reminder to periodically check shared bathrooms for objects that look subtly different from what you remember.

around.headline: Cross-country rally organisers booked over registration-fee scam
around.summary: Organisers of a cross-country rally in Karnataka have been booked after participants alleged they collected registration fees and failed to deliver on promises. Before paying any event registration fee, verify the organiser's track record and prefer traceable payment methods over cash.

around.headline: Metro Green Line disrupted by technical glitch
around.summary: BMRCL confirmed a technical glitch disrupted services on Namma Metro's Green Line today. If you rely on this line for your evening commute, check live status before heading to the station.

around.headline: Bengaluru reclaims 750 km of footpaths; night traffic curbs on Peenya flyover
around.summary: The city has reclaimed roughly 750 km of encroached footpaths, and new night-time traffic restrictions are now in force on the Peenya flyover. Pedestrians on reclaimed stretches should still watch for parked vehicles and construction debris during the transition.

around.headline: Air India flight hit by severe turbulence, 12 injured
around.summary: An Air India flight from Phuket to Delhi was hit by severe turbulence today, injuring 12 people on board. It's a good reminder to keep your seatbelt fastened during flights even when the sign is switched off.

street_smart.title: You take in a paying-guest tenant who shares the common bathroom in your home. One evening you notice the exhaust-fan cover looks slightly different from how you remember it — a small pinhole catches the light when you move past it. What do you do?
street_smart.based_on: Today's Bengaluru news: a software professional was arrested for secretly filming his landlady using a hidden camera in a shared bathroom (Deccan Herald, The Hindu, The News Minute). This hidden-camera/rented-housing privacy angle hasn't been used as a street-smart topic in the last 3 weeks — the closest recent rental scenario was a deposit dispute (July 16) and an eviction-notice scenario (July 30), both about money and tenancy terms, not surveillance.

choices.text: Assume you're imagining things since nothing looks like an obvious camera lens, and leave it alone.
choices.feedback: This is the trap. Hidden cameras are deliberately built into everyday objects — exhaust fans, smoke detectors, clocks, chargers, air fresheners — precisely so there's no obvious lens to spot. 'It doesn't look like a camera' is the design intent, not proof of safety.

choices.text: Confront the tenant alone right away and demand they explain or open the device.
choices.feedback: Risky. Confronting alone puts you in a direct, potentially unsafe standoff, and gives the person a chance to delete footage or swap out the device before there's any evidence to act on.

choices.text: Step out, discreetly scan the bathroom in low light with your phone's camera or a flashlight to check for a reflective glint, then call the police to report and let them search and seize the device.
choices.feedback: Correct. A working camera lens often reflects back as a small bright dot when scanned with a phone camera or flashlight in a dark room. Once you suspect a device, don't touch or remove it yourself — call the police so the search, seizure, and evidence chain are handled properly.

choices.text: Remove the device yourself and keep it as evidence, but say nothing to anyone for now while you decide what to do.
choices.feedback: Risky. Handling or storing the device yourself can break the evidence chain a prosecution would rely on, and delaying a report gives the person more time to cover their tracks elsewhere in the house.

takeaways: Hidden cameras are built into ordinary objects on purpose — treat anything that looks subtly different from what you remember buying as worth checking, not dismissing.
Quick check: in a dark room, slowly scan with your phone's camera or a flashlight held close to your eye — a working lens often shows up as a small bright reflective dot.
Don't confront alone or move the device — call the police (100/112) to search and seize it; tampering weakens the case and confrontation alone is a safety risk.

quiz.question: What disrupted Namma Metro's Green Line services in Bengaluru today, according to BMRCL?
options: A power outage across the city
quiz.why: BMRCL confirmed the disruption was a technical glitch rather than weather- or labour-related, which is why services were restored the same day once the fault was cleared.

quiz.question: Roughly how many kilometres of encroached footpaths has Bengaluru reclaimed as part of its recent civic drive?
quiz.why: The reclamation drive runs alongside new night-time traffic curbs on stretches like the Peenya flyover, part of a broader push to separate pedestrian and vehicle space in the city.

quiz.question: An Air India flight from Phuket to Delhi hit severe turbulence today, injuring how many people on board?
quiz.why: Clear-air turbulence can strike without warning on a smooth-looking flight, which is why airlines recommend keeping your seatbelt fastened at your seat even when the sign is switched off.

quiz.question: Bengaluru's notably cooler climate compared to most Indian cities owes largely to its elevation on which plateau?
quiz.why: Sitting at roughly 900 metres above sea level on the Deccan Plateau is why Bengaluru's evenings stay markedly cooler than coastal or plains cities even during peak summer.

quiz.question: Which single emergency helpline number was rolled out in India to unify police, fire, and ambulance services?
quiz.why: 112 was introduced under the Emergency Response Support System to be a single number for all emergencies, though legacy lines like 100 (police) and 108 (ambulance) still work in many states.
